conversation.content:
Hi there—congratulations on your new baby. My name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since delivery.

Today we’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question form that helps us tell the difference between the normal ups and downs of new motherhood and symptoms that might need a little extra support. The questions refer to the past seven days, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you. Everything you share is confidential, and we’ll go at whatever pace feels comfortable.

When you’re ready, I’ll ask the questions conversationally; you don’t need to worry about numbers or scoring. We’ll start gently. 

To begin: overall, in the past week, how much have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

[speaks softly, eyes on the blanket draped across my lap]

Honestly, Sarah… I can’t remember the last time I laughed. When my husband tries to joke—like he always used to—I just give him this half-smile so he won’t worry, but nothing feels funny anymore. Even those silly baby-animal videos that used to crack me up… they just seem flat now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

Not really… I mean, sometimes I’ll try to force a little laugh when my husband makes a joke, but it feels fake. Nothing actually feels funny inside. Even when the baby does something cute that would normally make me giggle, I just feel… empty.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice flat]

I can’t say I’ve looked forward to anything lately. My sister keeps texting about grabbing coffee or going for a walk, and I keep making excuses. Even simple stuff—watching my favorite show, a shower without rushing—sounds exhausting instead of enjoyable. Part of me wants to want those things, but the feeling never really shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[eyes drop to my hands, voice tight]

Yeah… a lot. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for two hours and I kept thinking, “I’m doing something wrong—other moms know how to soothe their babies.” When he finally slept I just sat there crying, convinced it’s my fault he was so upset. Even tiny things—like forgetting to put the diaper cream back in the caddy—turn into this loop of “I’m failing him already.”
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings the edge of the blanket]

Almost all the time. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly picture him choking—even though he’s latched fine—and my heart starts racing. At night I lie there listening to every squeak from the bassinet, sure something’s wrong. The other day I called the pediatrician because his poop looked a little green; the nurse was nice about it, but I felt ridiculous after. I know most of it’s “normal mom worry,” but it doesn’t feel normal in my body—my chest stays tight like I’m waiting for something awful to happen.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[hugs the blanket tighter, voice shaking]

Yes… especially when I’m alone with the baby. My heart starts racing and I feel like I can’t breathe, even though nothing’s happening. It’s like this wave of panic that he’ll stop breathing or something terrible will happen and I won’t know what to do. Sometimes I have to put him in the crib and go stand by the window just to catch my breath. There’s no real reason—it just hits out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

[nods, eyes glassy]

Most days, yeah. It feels like I’m drowning in small tasks—wash the bottles, answer one more text, fold the tiny socks—yet I can’t keep up. Yesterday I stood in front of the overflowing hamper just staring, too tired to move. If the baby stirs, my stomach drops because I’m already stretched so thin. I manage the basics, but everything feels ten times heavier, like I’m wading through thick mud while everyone else walks on pavement.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

[exhales slowly, looking exhausted]

Yeah… I’ll lie down and my mind just races. I keep replaying everything I did wrong that day—did I burp him long enough, did I miss a hunger cue—and the guilt keeps me wired. Even when the baby finally settles, I can’t drift off. Some nights I watch the clock slide past two, three, four… then it’s time to feed again and I haven’t slept at all. It’s like my body forgot how to let go.
I have felt sad or miserable

[presses lips together, eyes welling]

Pretty much every day. I wake up with this heavy feeling in my chest—like a gray cloud settled over me and won’t lift. Sometimes I’ll be holding the baby and tears just start rolling down my face for no clear reason. I keep telling myself I should be grateful—he’s healthy, I’m not alone—but the sadness just sits there. It’s exhausting pretending everything’s okay when inside I feel so… empty and low.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[quiet for a moment, then nods]

Yeah… it’s happened a few times this week. Day before yesterday I finally got him down for a nap and instead of resting I just sat on the couch and started sobbing. I couldn’t even tell my husband why when he walked in—just kept saying “I’m tired.” It feels like the tears come whenever there’s a tiny break in the chaos, like my body’s waiting for a pause to let it all out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly, eyes widening]

No—never that. I’ve felt overwhelmed and hopeless, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

You've shared how the joy and color seem to have drained from everyday moments since your baby arrived: jokes feel forced, small tasks feel monumental, and a heavy sadness settles in even when you think you "should" feel grateful. Nights are long with racing thoughts, and sudden waves of panic make you step away from your baby just to breathe-yet you're clear that keeping him safe remains your north star.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to feel genuine amusement or joy, describing laughter as forced and feeling "empty"</sym>, <sym>Patient conveys near-complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, consistent with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive self-blame for routine infant distress and trivial oversights, consistent with "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intrusive, physical anxiety occurring "almost all the time" with racing heart and constant tension, clearly matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic episodes occurring "quite a lot" when alone with baby, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to complete simple tasks, immobilized by laundry, and dreading infant needs—matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly insomnia driven by racing anxious thoughts and guilt, watching the clock until dawn—clearly "most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent daily sadness, spontaneous tears, and an unshakeable low mood matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes this week, specifically triggered by quiet moments, indicating frequent crying but not most of the time.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Every item on the EPDS except self-harm was endorsed at the highest or near-highest level: loss of pleasure and laughter, pervasive self-blame, near-nightly insomnia, frequent crying, and multiple panic attacks. A score of 26 far exceeds the ≥14 threshold for "probable major depression" in postpartum women. Symptoms map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest/pleasure, fatigue, feelings of worthlessness, diminished concentration, and recurrent panic-like anxiety. No suicidal ideation was endorsed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> within one week
2. Request evaluation for both <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>postpartum anxiety</med>/panic disorder
3. Discuss treatment options: individual therapy, possible antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding, and/or short-term anti-anxiety medication
4. Plan daily support: partner/family to handle one night feeding so you can obtain a 4-5 hour stretch of sleep
5. Schedule brief daily check-ins (text or call) with a trusted friend or relative for the next two weeks
6. Provide written list of 24/7 crisis lines (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and instruct to call if distress escalates
7. Re-screen with EPDS at two weeks to monitor symptom trajectory after intervention
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother (infant age not specified)  
Date: [today]  
Screener: [therapist name], LCSW  

I. Responses consistent with EPDS items  
- Item 1 (laughter/pleasure): Marked loss; describes “empty,” forced affect  
- Item 2 (enjoyment): Anhedonia; avoids previously pleasant activities  
- Item 3 (self-blame): Excessive guilt, catastrophizing routine infant care  
- Item 4 (anxiety): Persistent, intrusive “what-if” worries, somatic tension  
- Item 5 (panic): Sudden autonomic surges, safety behaviors (putting baby down, standing by window)  
- Item 6 (coping): Feels “drowning,” tasks “ten-times heavier,” low energy  
- Item 7 (sleep): Initial insomnia driven by rumination, guilt review  
- Item 8 (sad mood): Daily low mood, affect lability, tearfulness  
- Item 9 (crying): Frequent crying spells, often unprovoked  
- Item 10 (self-harm): Denies; no suicidal ideation endorsed  

II. Pattern summary  
Prominent depressive symptoms (anhedonia, low mood, guilt, tearfulness) co-occurring with significant anxiety/panic; functional impairment in sleep, self-care, and infant-care confidence. No self-harm ideation.  

III. Screening significance / risk flags  
- Meets probable cutoff for major depressive symptoms in postpartum context  
- Anxiety symptoms exceed “typical” new-parent worry; possible comorbid postpartum anxiety or panic  
- Maternal fatigue and low confidence may impact bonding and infant safety  

IV. Next steps recommended  
1. Complete EPDS scoring; document numerical score  
2. Arrange same-week follow-up (office or tele-health) for symptom review and safety check  
3. Provide postpartum depression/anxiety psycho-education and support resources  
4. Consider referral to perinatal mental health specialist for evaluation of diagnosis and treatment options  
5. Continue routine safety monitoring; instruct to seek immediate care if suicidal thoughts develop
